currency_note: Financial statements are prepared and reported in RMB (Renminbi/CNY); the ADS (one ADS = one ordinary share) trades in USD on Nasdaq (TCOM) and in HKD on HKEX (9961). DCF modeling must convert RMB cash flows to USD at a forecast USD/RMB rate rather than treating reported figures as USD-native -- the company itself dual-reports RMB and USD-converted figures each quarter at the then-prevailing Fed Reserve rate (e.g. USD1.00=RMB6.7851 on June 30, 2026), which is a translation convenience, not a hedge.
overview: Trip.com Group Limited is a Cayman Islands holding company that is the leading online travel platform in China and one of the largest globally, operating through the Ctrip, Qunar, Trip.com, and Skyscanner brands. It is a one-stop travel service provider covering accommodation reservations, transportation ticketing, packaged tours, and corporate travel management, serving both leisure and business travelers in China and, increasingly, internationally. Operations in China are conducted through PRC subsidiaries and VIE (variable interest entity) contractual arrangements rather than direct equity ownership, reflecting PRC restrictions on foreign investment in internet businesses.

business_model.summary: Trip.com earns commission- and fee-based revenue by aggregating hotel, flight, rail, package-tour and corporate travel supply and monetizing bookings made through its platforms. Revenue is overwhelmingly transactional (take-rate on gross bookings) rather than subscription-based, making it highly sensitive to travel volume. Domestic China travel (Ctrip/Qunar brands) remains the core profit engine while the Trip.com-branded international OTA and inbound-China travel are the fastest-growing segments.

revenue_streams.name: Accommodation reservation
revenue_streams.description: Commissions on hotel and other lodging bookings; largest and fastest-scaling segment, FY2025 RMB26.1bn, +21% YoY

revenue_streams.name: Transportation ticketing
revenue_streams.description: Commissions/fees on air, rail and other transport bookings; FY2025 RMB22.5bn, +11% YoY

revenue_streams.name: Packaged tours
revenue_streams.description: FY2025 RMB4.7bn, +8% YoY; more cyclical/seasonal than other lines

revenue_streams.name: Corporate travel management
revenue_streams.description: B2B managed travel services for enterprise clients; FY2025 RMB2.8bn, +13% YoY

revenue_streams.name: Other (advertising, financial services)
revenue_streams.description: Online advertising placements for travel suppliers and financial services; FY2025 ~RMB6.4bn

business_model.customer_type: Primarily B2C (individual leisure and business travelers) with a growing B2B corporate-travel-management offering for enterprise clients; supply side is B2B (hotels, airlines, tour operators) monetized via commissions, advertising and traffic-allocation fees
business_model.geographic_mix: Mainland China remains the large majority of revenue and profit (domestic OTA via Ctrip/Qunar); international business (Trip.com-branded OTA outside China, Skyscanner, inbound travel into China) is the smallest but fastest-growing component -- international platform revenue grew >50% YoY in Q2 2026 and gross bookings grew ~65% YoY in Q1 2026, while inbound travel bookings surged ~90-100% YoY across 2025-2026

main_competitors: Meituan (travel vertical of China's largest local-services/food-delivery super-app)
Qunar (Trip.com's own value-brand, also independently competes with budget OTAs)
Booking Holdings / Expedia (international OTA competition for outbound and global travelers)
MakeMyTrip (competes for South/Southeast Asia and some overlapping inbound/outbound corridors)
competitive_position.market_position: Dominant leader in China's OTA market -- cited as the top choice for roughly 68.7% of Chinese travelers surveyed in 2025, with an estimated ~56% share of China's online hotel/travel booking market per regulatory findings. Trip.com Group accounts for an estimated ~13% of the global OTA market, making it one of the largest travel platforms worldwide behind Booking Holdings and Expedia.

moat_factors.description: Largest hotel and flight inventory aggregation in China; scale lets it negotiate better rates and secure exclusive or preferential inventory, though this exact practice (exclusivity + 'lowest price across the internet' clauses) triggered the 2026 SAMR antitrust penalty
Ctrip is a legacy, trusted brand in China dating to 1999; Trip.com brand is being built internationally; Skyscanner gives flight-metasearch brand recognition outside China

More travelers attract more hotel/airline supply and vice versa, but Chinese regulators' finding that Trip.com used traffic-allocation and technical measures to lock in exclusivity suggests the network effect was partly reinforced by anti-competitive means now under regulatory remedy
Heavy R&D/product-development spend (~24-26% of revenue) funds AI-driven personalization, customer service and itinerary tools across the booking funnel

Consumer switching costs are low (price comparison across apps is easy); some loyalty-program and corporate-travel-contract stickiness exists but is not a strong moat versus Meituan's super-app bundling or Alibaba's ecosystem

weaknesses: Heavy reliance on discretionary Chinese consumer and business travel spending, which is cyclical and was devastated during COVID-19 lockdowns (2020-2022)

Core China accommodation/ticketing business is now under a formal antitrust remedy order restricting the exclusivity and pricing practices that helped build its market position, raising execution risk around unwinding hotel contracts
International (Trip.com-branded) business, while growing fast, is still sub-scale versus Booking.com/Expedia/Agoda outside Asia and faces intense price competition
Regulatory and reputational scrutiny (SAMR investigation, broader China tech-platform 'anti-involution' campaign) could recur and extend to further practices or peers-driven price wars

Dependent on third-party travel suppliers (airlines, hotels, rail) for inventory and pricing; margin is a function of commission rates set partly by negotiating leverage now constrained by the antitrust order

growth_drivers: Outbound and cross-border China travel normalization/growth well above pre-COVID (2019) levels -- outbound flight and hotel bookings reached ~140% of 2019 volumes in Q3 2025

Inbound travel into China as a structural growth driver: ~20 million inbound travelers served in 2025 with a stated 5-year ambition to reach 200 million, aided by visa-free policies and the 'Taste of China' program

International expansion of the Trip.com-branded OTA outside Greater China: international platform revenue +50%+ YoY and gross bookings +60-65% YoY through 2025-2026, now management's primary growth engine, explicitly growing faster than the group average

AI integration across the travel journey (search, personalization, customer service, itinerary planning) under the 'Globalization and Great Quality' (G2) strategic framework articulated by Executive Chairman James Liang
Corporate travel management (TMC) segment growth (+13-20% YoY) as Chinese and multinational enterprises re-normalize business travel budgets
Secular rise of Chinese outbound/inbound tourism as a share of global travel, and continued penetration of online booking versus offline travel agents in China and Asia

business.description: Meituan's super-app bundling (travel + food delivery + local services), Alibaba's Fliggy, and Tencent-backed Tongcheng-Elong all compete aggressively on price and traffic; Beijing's 'anti-involution' campaign signals regulators may also target competitors, potentially triggering further price wars

The 2026 SAMR order requires Trip.com to cease exclusivity and 'lowest price across the internet' arrangements with hotels and refund deposits; unwinding these practices could reduce negotiating leverage and compress take-rates in the core accommodation business
COVID-19 demonstrated the business can see bookings collapse almost overnight; similar risk from future pandemics, geopolitical conflict, terrorism, or natural disasters disrupting travel
Reliance on airlines, hotels, and rail operators for inventory; commission structures are subject to renegotiation and supplier consolidation

financial.description: All operations and revenue are RMB-denominated while the ADS trades in USD; RMB depreciation reduces USD-translated earnings and ADS value even if local operating performance is strong

Company carries exchangeable senior notes and short/long-term debt (~RMB26bn short-term + modest long-term debt as of mid-2026); fair-value changes in these instruments create non-operating P&L volatility reflected in non-GAAP add-backs

financial.risk: Large one-off and non-operating items distort reported earnings
financial.description: FY2025 net income was boosted by a ~RMB19.9bn one-time investment gain; Q2 2026 net income swung to a loss from the RMB5.2bn SAMR fine -- both complicate clean earnings trend analysis for valuation

regulatory.description: RMB5.2bn (~US$770m) SAMR fine in 2026 for monopolistic conduct (exclusive hotel deals, 'lowest price' clauses, traffic-allocation abuse); represents ~7.5% of 2025 Mainland China revenue and signals ongoing regulatory risk for dominant platforms in China

Trip.com Group is a Cayman Islands holding company with no direct equity ownership of its PRC operating entities, relying on VIE contractual arrangements because PRC law restricts foreign ownership of internet businesses; PRC authorities could invalidate or restrict this structure, which would materially impair the value of the ADSs

Holding Foreign Companies Accountable Act risk persists if PCAOB inspection access to China-based auditors were again restricted; mitigated by Trip.com's dual listing on HKEX (9961) since 2021, which provides a liquidity backstop if Nasdaq trading were disrupted
China's data localization and cybersecurity regulations affect how travel and personal data can be processed and transferred, particularly relevant given the international expansion strategy

macro.description: Domestic travel demand is tied to Chinese consumer confidence and discretionary income; a property-sector-driven or broader economic slowdown in China would pressure bookings
Broader geopolitical friction can affect outbound Chinese travel patterns, cross-border capital flows, and sentiment toward China-domiciled ADRs independent of company fundamentals
Company specifically cited 'elevated energy prices' as a macro headwind weighing on Q2 2026 transportation-ticketing revenue and overall growth deceleration
International/outbound exposure ties results to global travel demand, which is sensitive to recessions, currency moves affecting travel affordability, and public health events

execution.description: Co-founders Min Fan (resigned as director and president) and Qi Ji (resigned as director) departed the board in February 2026, with two new independent directors appointed; while framed as routine governance refresh, leadership transitions at this scale warrant monitoring

Successfully competing with entrenched global OTAs (Booking, Expedia, Agoda) outside Asia while simultaneously defending domestic share against Meituan/Alibaba/Tencent-backed rivals requires sustained, well-capitalized execution across very different markets

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Global and Asian online travel markets are in secular growth, with China's outbound/inbound travel structurally rebuilding well past pre-COVID 2019 levels (outbound bookings ~140% of 2019 volume in Q3 2025) and inbound travel targeted to grow 10x over five years (20m to 200m visitors). Online penetration of travel bookings continues to rise versus offline agents, particularly in China and emerging Asia.
macro_factors.cyclicality: High -- travel is discretionary consumer/business spending, highly exposed to macro downturns, pandemics, and geopolitical shocks (demonstrated dramatically in 2020-2022); revenue mix is almost entirely transactional/booking-volume-based rather than recurring/subscription
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Low-to-moderate direct exposure (modest debt load, large net cash position of ~RMB100bn+ in cash/short-term investments as of mid-2026 which benefits from higher rates on interest income); moderate indirect sensitivity via consumer discretionary spending and ADR valuation multiples
macro_factors.currency_exposure: High -- functional/reporting currency is RMB, but ADS trades in USD (and HKD on HKEX); RMB/USD movements directly affect USD-translated revenue, earnings and the per-ADS figures investors see, independent of underlying business performance
key_input_costs: Product development/engineering talent costs (~24-26% of revenue)
Sales and marketing/customer acquisition spend (~24-29% of revenue, elevated amid competitive pricing environment)
Payment processing and cost of revenue tied to booking volume
macro_factors.regulatory_trend: Intensifying -- China's 'anti-involution' campaign against excessive platform competition, the 2026 SAMR antitrust fine, and the ongoing SAMR investigation into dominant-position abuse all point to a more restrictive regulatory environment for large Chinese internet platforms, with potential for similar scrutiny of Meituan and other peers

recent_developments.event: Q2 2026 results: total net revenue RMB15.7bn (+6% YoY), but reported a net loss of RMB2.4bn (vs. net income RMB4.9bn in Q2 2025) due to the RMB5.2bn SAMR anti-monopoly penalty; excluding the fine, net income would have been RMB2.7bn. International platform revenue grew >50% YoY and inbound travel revenue grew at a high double-digit rate.

SAMR formally concluded its investigation and imposed a RMB5.2 billion (~US$770 million) fine -- China's largest platform antitrust penalty since Alibaba's 2021 fine -- for monopolistic conduct including exclusive hotel dealing arrangements, 'lowest price across the internet' clauses, and traffic-allocation abuse; Trip.com was ordered to refund ~RMB122m in hotel security deposits and disgorge ~RMB1,658m of gains, with the balance as fines.

Q1 2026 results: total net revenues RMB16.2bn (+17% YoY); international gross bookings +65% YoY, inbound bookings +90% YoY; management guided Q2 2026 revenue growth to decelerate sharply to just 3-8% YoY, citing macro headwinds (energy prices, geopolitical volatility) and 'operational adjustments... to align with evolving industry standards and compliance frameworks' -- a clear reference to the looming SAMR outcome.

Q4/FY2025 results: FY2025 revenue RMB62.4bn (+17% YoY), FY2025 net income RMB33.4bn (boosted by a ~RMB19.9bn one-time investment gain); board changes announced with co-founders Min Fan (President) and Qi Ji resigning from the board, replaced by two new independent directors (May Yihong Wu, Iris Yang Xiao).

Trip.com Group received formal notice from SAMR that it had commenced an antitrust investigation into alleged abuse of dominant market position, which the company disclosed it was 'fully cooperating' with; this preceded the July 2026 fine.

Q3 2025 results: record quarterly net revenue of RMB18.3bn (+16% YoY); international OTA bookings +60% YoY, inbound travel bookings +100%+ YoY, outbound bookings reaching ~140% of 2019 pre-COVID volumes.

guidance.as_of: Q1 2026 earnings release (2026-06-24), reiterated/realized in Q2 2026 release (2026-09-15)

items.notes: Sharply down from the +17% YoY growth delivered in Q1 2026; management cited macro headwinds (elevated energy prices, geopolitical volatility) plus 'operational adjustments...to align with evolving industry standards and compliance frameworks' -- i.e., anticipated changes stemming from the SAMR investigation. Actual Q2 2026 revenue growth came in at +6% YoY, within the guided range.

items.target: Corresponding compression expected alongside slower revenue growth
items.notes: No specific margin number given, but management explicitly flagged margin and bottom-line impact alongside the growth deceleration; realized result was a GAAP net loss due to the SAMR fine, though adjusted EBITDA margin held at 29% (down from 33% in Q2 2025 and 30% in Q1 2026).

items.target: ~200 million inbound travelers over five years
items.notes: Stated strategic ambition reiterated across multiple quarters as a structural growth driver; not a formal financial guidance metric but a company-disclosed KPI target

guidance.management_commentary: Executive Chairman James Liang has repeatedly framed strategy around 'Globalization and Great Quality' (G2), emphasizing AI investment across the travel journey and international expansion. CEO Jane Sun's Q2 2026 commentary acknowledged a need to 'build a healthier ecosystem centered on value, experience, and service quality' -- language that aligns with accepting the SAMR-mandated changes to hotel-partner practices -- while stressing 'disciplined execution' going forward. No specific full-year 2026 revenue or margin guidance figure has been issued as of the most recent (Q2 2026) release; management's language suggests continued caution about near-term growth deceleration as the business adjusts to the post-SAMR operating framework.

bull_case: Dominant, scaled leader (~56-69% share by various measures) in China's large and still-underpenetrated online travel market, with multiple growth vectors (domestic recovery, outbound, inbound, international) still in double-digit-plus growth as of 2025

International (Trip.com-branded) business is compounding rapidly (50-65%+ YoY bookings/revenue growth) off a low base, offering a long runway largely independent of China-specific regulatory risk, diversifying the revenue base over time

Structural inbound-travel tailwind (visa-free policy support, 'Taste of China' program) with a stated ambition to 10x inbound travelers over five years, a segment growing 90-100%+ YoY and less exposed to domestic competitive intensity

Strong balance sheet with ~RMB100bn+ (~US$15bn) in cash, short-term investments and time deposits as of mid-2026, providing ample flexibility for buybacks, M&A, or absorbing one-off shocks like the SAMR fine without balance-sheet strain

The SAMR fine, while painful, resolves a multi-quarter regulatory overhang (investigation opened January 2026, concluded July 2026); removal of exclusivity practices could, over time, normalize competitive dynamics across all OTAs rather than singling out Trip.com
bear_case: China platform-antitrust risk is recurring, not one-and-done: the 'anti-involution' campaign suggests further regulatory actions against Trip.com or sector-wide price wars among Meituan/Alibaba/Tencent-backed rivals remain plausible, and the mandated end of exclusivity/'lowest price' arrangements could structurally compress the take-rate advantage that underpinned Trip.com's dominant share

Revenue growth has decelerated sharply and unpredictably -- from +17% YoY in Q1 2026 to a guided +3-8% for Q2 2026 -- with management explicitly linking the slowdown to compliance/regulatory adjustments, making near-term forecasting unusually uncertain

VIE structure and HFCAA/geopolitical risk remain structural overhangs for any US-listed China ADR; while the Hong Kong dual-listing mitigates pure delisting risk, VIE invalidation risk is not fully hedge-able and is a binary tail risk

Reported earnings have been volatile and hard to interpret cleanly -- FY2025 net income was flattered by a ~RMB19.9bn one-off investment gain, while Q2 2026 swung to a net loss from the RMB5.2bn SAMR fine -- obscuring underlying operating trends for investors and complicating valuation

Heavy reliance on discretionary Chinese and global travel spending leaves the business exposed to any renewed macro shock (economic slowdown in China, geopolitical escalation, energy price spikes, or a future public-health event), with COVID-19 having already demonstrated the magnitude of downside risk to bookings
